q: Who is the author of the story "Footprints Without Feet"?
o: H. G. Wells
Robert W. Peterson
Guy de Maupassant
Ruskin Bond
e: "Footprints Without Feet" is written by famous British science-fiction author H. G. Wells, adapted from his novel "The Invisible Man".

q: What did the two boys in London suddenly see on the steps of a house?
o: Drops of red paint
A pile of stolen clothes
A stray invisible dog
Fresh muddy imprints of a pair of bare feet
e: The two boys were amazed to see fresh muddy imprints of a pair of bare feet appearing on the steps without any visible person.

q: What was the name of the eccentric scientist who discovered how to make the human body invisible?
o: Ausable
Jaffers
Griffin
Ebright
e: Griffin was the scientist who carried out experiments and swallowed rare drugs to make his body transparent as glass.

q: How did Griffin make his body invisible?
o: By wearing a magic cloak
By swallowing certain rare drugs
By standing inside an X-ray chamber
By applying herbal ointment
e: Griffin finally swallowed certain rare drugs that made his body transparent as a sheet of glass, though solid as glass.

q: Why did Griffin set fire to his landlord's house in London?
o: To test a new chemical fuel
Because the landlord disliked him and tried to eject him
By accident while cooking dinner
To hide stolen jewels inside
e: Griffin's landlord disliked him and tried to eject him, so in revenge Griffin set fire to the house and slipped away invisibly.

q: During which time of the year did Griffin wander naked and invisible in London?
o: Mid-winter in January
Rainy autumn in October
Warm spring in April
Hot summer in July
e: It was mid-winter (January), and the air was bitterly cold, making it miserable for Griffin to wander without clothes.

q: Where did Griffin first slip in for warmth and clothes after becoming invisible?
o: A railway waiting room
A museum hall
A village church
A big London store
e: Griffin slipped into a big London store at closing time to get warm clothes and food without paying.

q: In which street in London did Griffin find a theatrical company shop for bandages and disguise?
o: Fleet Street
Baker Street
Drury Lane
Oxford Street
e: Griffin hurried to Drury Lane, the centre of the theatre world, and entered a theatrical company shop.

q: What is the name of the village to which Griffin travelled by train to escape London?
o: Sussex
Reading
Iping
Silli
e: Eager to get away from crowded London, Griffin took a train to the quiet village of Iping.

q: How many rooms did Griffin book at the local inn in Iping?
o: One room
Two rooms
Three rooms
Four rooms
e: Griffin booked two rooms at the local inn in Iping and paid Mrs. Hall in advance.

q: Who was the landlord's wife at the inn in Iping?
o: Mrs. Hall
Mme Forestier
Miss Mason
Mrs. Pumphrey
e: Mrs. Hall was the landlord's wife who tried to be friendly with the strange scientist at her inn.

q: Whose house was burgled early in the morning in Iping?
o: The magistrate's house
The baker's house
The village doctor's house
The clergyman's house
e: A clergyman and his wife were awakened by noises in their study and discovered housekeeping money missing from the desk.

q: What was the name of the village constable in Iping?
o: Mr. Weiherer
Mr. Keesing
Mr. Herriot
Mr. Jaffers
e: Mr. Jaffers was the village constable sent for to arrest the mysterious stranger.

q: In "Footprints Without Feet", what did Mrs. Hall's bedroom chair do when she entered Griffin's room?
o: It caught fire on the carpet
It broke into pieces immediately
It sprang into the air and charged straight at her
It slid quietly into the cupboard
e: The bedroom chair became alive, sprang into the air, charged straight at Mrs. Hall, and pushed both Hall and his wife out.

q: According to the JAC PYQ description from the story, Griffin was a brilliant scientist, yet what kind of person was he?
o: A generous philanthropist
A rather lawless person
A timid schoolteacher
A humble clergyman
e: The textbook explicitly notes: "Griffin, the scientist, had carried out experiment after experiment... brilliant scientist though he was, Griffin was rather a lawless person."

q: Who is the author of the biographical chapter "The Making of a Scientist"?
o: Robert W. Peterson
K. A. Abbas
Claire Boiko
H. G. Wells
e: "The Making of a Scientist" is written by Robert W. Peterson, chronicling the early life and scientific journey of Richard H. Ebright.

q: At what age did Richard Ebright excite the scientific world with his new theory on how cells work?
o: Age 22
Age 30
Age 18
Age 15
e: At the age of twenty-two, former "scout of the year" Richard H. Ebright excited the scientific world with a new theory on how cells work.

q: Where did Richard Ebright grow up?
o: In central London, England
Near Boston, Massachusetts
South of Toronto, Canada
North of Reading, Pennsylvania
e: Richard Ebright grew up north of Reading, Pennsylvania, where there wasn't much he could do outdoors with no playmates.

q: How many species of butterflies had Ebright collected by the time he was in second grade?
o: Ten species
Twelve species
Twenty-five species
Fifty species
e: By the time he was in the second grade, Ebright had collected all twenty-five species of butterflies found around his hometown.

q: Which children's book did Ebright's mother give him that opened the world of science to him?
o: The Origin of Species
The Travels of Monarch X
Butterflies of North America
Secrets of the Cell
e: His mother got him a children's book called "The Travels of Monarch X", which described how monarch butterflies migrate to Central America.

q: Where do monarch butterflies migrate according to "The Travels of Monarch X"?
o: South Africa
Central America
Northern Canada
Western Europe
e: The book explained how monarch butterflies migrate from North America to Central America.

q: Who was the scientist at the University of Toronto for whom Ebright tagged monarch butterflies?
o: Dr. Frederick A. Urquhart
Mr. Richard A. Weiherer
James R. Wong
Dr. Robert Peterson
e: Readers of "The Travels of Monarch X" were invited to tag butterflies for research by Dr. Frederick A. Urquhart of the University of Toronto, Canada.

q: What did Richard Ebright show as his entry in the seventh-grade county science fair where he lost?
o: A working telescope model
A jar of monarch caterpillars
A collection of twenty-five coins
Slides of frog tissues under a microscope
e: In seventh grade, Ebright's entry was slides of frog tissues shown under a microscope, and he lost because it was a display rather than a real experiment.

q: According to Ebright's high school project, which butterfly species was believed to copy the monarch?
o: Gossamer-winged butterfly
Swallowtail butterfly
Viceroy butterfly
Painted Lady butterfly
e: Ebright tested the theory that viceroy butterflies copy monarchs because monarchs taste bad to birds while viceroys taste good.

q: How many tiny gold spots are there on a monarch pupa?
o: Eighteen
Six
Twelve
Twenty-five
e: In his second year of high school, Ebright investigated the purpose of the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa.

q: What did Ebright discover the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa actually produce?
o: A poisonous fluid against birds
A hormone necessary for the butterfly's full development
Pure gold dust for camouflage
Food for winter hibernation
e: Ebright and another excellent science student built a device proving the gold spots produced a hormone essential for the butterfly's full development.

q: Who was Richard Ebright's college room-mate who co-wrote the famous DNA cell theory paper with him?
o: James R. Wong
Richard Weiherer
Robert Peterson
Frederick Urquhart
e: Ebright and his college room-mate James R. Wong worked all night drawing pictures and building plastic models of molecules, then wrote the paper together.

q: In which prestigious scientific journal was Ebright and Wong's paper on cell theory published?
o: Journal of American Biology
Harvard Science Review
Nature Weekly
Proceedings of the National Academy of Science
e: Their paper appeared in the "Proceedings of the National Academy of Science", the first time that journal had ever published college students' work.

q: Which substance in the nucleus of a cell is called the "blueprint for life" in the chapter?
o: Insulin
Chlorophyll
Glucose
DNA
e: DNA is the substance in the nucleus of a cell that controls heredity, determines cell form and function, and is called the blueprint for life.

q: Who was Richard A. Weiherer in Richard Ebright's life?
o: A professor at Toronto University
His biology lab partner
His social studies teacher and adviser to Debating and Model UN clubs
His father's lawyer
e: Richard A. Weiherer was Ebright's social studies teacher and adviser to both the Debating and Model United Nations clubs.

q: Even though Griffin's body became transparent as a sheet of glass, what physical property did it still retain?
o: It could pass through brick walls
It remained as solid as glass
It floated above the ground
It glowed faintly in darkness
e: The text states that Griffin's body became as transparent as a sheet of glass — though it also remained as solid as glass.

q: How did Griffin remain invisible only when he had no clothes on?
o: His drugs worked only on skin, not on cloth
He forgot to spray the medicine on his coat
His clothes turned bright white at night
Cloth absorbs heat and reverses invisibility
e: The rare drugs made only Griffin's body transparent; any clothes he put on remained completely visible, making him look like a dressed man or headless figure.

q: What did Griffin eat and drink inside the big London store after closing time?
o: Cold meat and coffee, followed by sweets and wine
Roast chicken and lemonade
Apples, biscuits, and warm milk
Bread, cheese, and hot tea
e: In the kitchen of the restaurant, he consumed cold meat and coffee, and followed up the meal with sweets and wine taken from the grocery store.

q: Where did Griffin fall asleep inside the London store, causing him to wake up late the next morning?
o: Under a dining table
Inside a changing room
Behind a wooden counter
On a pile of quilts
e: Exhausted and full, Griffin finally settled down to sleep on a pile of quilts and did not wake up before the assistants arrived next morning.

q: How did Griffin manage to escape when two assistants chased him in the London store?
o: He bribed them with stolen coins
He locked them inside a cupboard
He quickly took off his newly found clothes
He jumped out of a second-floor window
e: Panicked, Griffin could escape only by quickly taking off his newly found clothes, becoming invisible once more in the chill January air.

q: What items did Griffin wear from the Drury Lane theatrical shop to disguise his empty head and face?
o: A soldier's helmet and velvet mask
Bandages round his forehead, dark glasses, false nose, big bushy side-whiskers, and a large hat
A woollen scarf, hood, and riding boots
A clown wig and painted spectacles
e: He emerged wearing bandages round his forehead, dark glasses, a false nose, big bushy side-whiskers, and a large hat.

q: How did Griffin treat the shopkeeper in Drury Lane before leaving?
o: He promised to pay by cheque
He callously attacked him from behind and robbed all the money he could find
He thanked him and left a gold watch
He locked him politely in the cellar
e: To escape without being seen, Griffin callously attacked the shopkeeper from behind and robbed him of all the money he could find.

q: What excuse did Griffin give Mrs. Hall for his bandaged face and rude desire to be left alone?
o: He desired solitude for his work and an accident had affected his face
He had taken a religious vow of silence
He was hiding from dangerous criminals
He was recovering from infectious smallpox
e: Griffin told Mrs. Hall his reason for coming to Iping was a desire for solitude and that an accident had affected his face.

q: Why was Mrs. Hall initially willing to excuse Griffin's strange habits and irritable temper?
o: Because the clergyman recommended him
Because he promised to cure her illness
Because he was an old friend of her husband
Because she was satisfied that her guest was an eccentric scientist and he had paid her in advance
e: Satisfied that her guest was an eccentric scientist, and in view of the fact that he had paid her in advance, Mrs. Hall excused his strange habits.

q: What weapon did the clergyman firmly grasp in his hand when he crept downstairs to catch the burglar?
o: An iron key
A pistol
A poker
A wooden stick
e: With a poker grasped firmly in his hand, the clergyman flung open the study door shouting "Surrender!" only to find the room empty.

q: When Mr. and Mrs. Hall entered Griffin's room, what convinced them that he had been up for some time?
o: His suitcase had disappeared
The window curtains were torn
The bedclothes were cold
A candle was still burning
e: They noticed the bedclothes were cold, showing that the scientist must have been up for some time, and his bandages lay about the room.

q: What strange belief did Mrs. Hall hold when the furniture in Griffin's room attacked her?
o: That an earthquake had struck Iping
That the room was haunted by spirits brought into her furniture by the stranger
That burglars were hiding inside the mattress
That her husband was playing a prank
e: Mrs. Hall fell down the stairs in hysterics, convinced that the room was haunted by spirits that the stranger had caused to enter her furniture.

q: What finally confirmed the neighbours' suspicion that Griffin was behind the burglary at the clergyman's home?
o: He suddenly produced some ready cash after admitting earlier that he had no money
He was caught climbing the clergyman's wall
He left muddy footprints inside the church
He wore the clergyman's coat in public
e: Suspicion grew stronger when Griffin suddenly produced some ready cash, even though he had admitted not long before that he had no money.

q: How long did it take Griffin to become a "headless man" before the horrified people in the bar?
o: Ten minutes
Almost an hour
Half an hour
Only a minute
e: Suddenly he threw off bandages, whiskers, spectacles, and even nose — it took him only a minute to do this, revealing a headless man.

q: What happened to Constable Jaffers at the end of the struggle with the unseen Griffin?
o: He ran away in terror
He arrested Mrs. Hall by mistake
He handcuffed Griffin successfully
He was knocked unconscious
e: As Jaffers made a last attempt to hold on to the unseen scientist, he was knocked unconscious and Griffin shook himself free.

q: Why could Richard Ebright not play football or baseball as a child north of Reading?
o: There were no playgrounds in Pennsylvania
He had a weak leg from an illness
He was an only child with no teammates around to form a team
His mother forbade outdoor sports
e: There wasn't much he could do in Reading as an only child — "I certainly couldn't play football or baseball with a team of one," he recalled.

q: Besides butterflies, what other items did Ebright collect as a young boy?
o: Stamps, feathers, and shells
Rocks, fossils, and coins
Dry leaves, beetles, and keys
Maps, postcards, and badges
e: Beginning in kindergarten, Ebright collected butterflies as well as rocks, fossils, and coins, and also became an eager astronomer.

q: When did Richard Ebright's father pass away?
o: When Richard was in third grade
When Richard entered seventh grade
During Richard's freshman year at Harvard
When Richard was in kindergarten
e: Ebright's father died when he was in third grade, after which his mother became his whole support and learning companion.

q: How long did the butterfly collecting season around Reading last each year?
o: Only six weeks in late summer
Three weeks in early winter
Ten weeks in mid-spring
Six months from spring to autumn
e: The butterfly collecting season around Reading lasts only six weeks in late summer, so chasing them one by one yielded too few.

q: Why did Ebright begin raising a flock of monarch butterflies in his basement?
o: To protect them from freezing winter snow
Because Dr. Urquhart paid him per wing
To sell them at the county fair
Because chasing butterflies one by one during the short six-week season wouldn't let him tag many
e: Since the collecting season lasted only six weeks, he caught a female monarch, took her eggs, and raised thousands through their life cycle in his basement.

q: Why did Ebright eventually lose interest in tagging monarch butterflies?
o: Monarchs stopped visiting Pennsylvania
His mother sold his equipment
It was tedious and offered little feedback — only two of his tagged butterflies were recaptured within 75 miles
Dr. Urquhart retired from Toronto University
e: Tagging was tedious with little feedback: only two butterflies he tagged were ever recaptured, and neither was more than seventy-five miles from home.

q: What crucial lesson did losing the seventh-grade county science fair teach Richard Ebright?
o: Never to use a microscope at fairs
That real science requires doing actual experiments, not just making a neat display
To focus solely on astronomy instead of biology
That judges only reward large colourful charts
e: Seeing everyone else win while he got nothing taught Ebright that winners had tried to do real experiments, not simply make a neat display.

q: In his eighth-grade project, what did Ebright suspect might carry the viral disease killing monarch caterpillars?
o: A mosquito
A beetle
A starling bird
A honeybee
e: Ebright thought the viral disease killing monarch caterpillars every few years might be carried by a beetle, so he raised caterpillars in the presence of beetles.

q: What surprising discovery did Ebright make while testing whether birds eat monarch butterflies?
o: A starling refused ordinary bird food and ate all the monarchs it could get
Birds only ate viceroys and never touched monarchs
Monarchs attacked and chased away the starlings
Birds died instantly after tasting a monarch
e: Ebright found that a starling would not eat ordinary bird food; instead, it would eat all the monarchs it could get.

q: At which army institute did Ebright get a chance to work during the summer after winning at the International Science Fair?
o: Johns Hopkins Defence Centre
National Naval Entomology Wing
West Point Military Lab
Walter Reed Army Institute of Research
e: Winning third place in zoology at the International Science and Engineering Fair earned him a summer opportunity at the entomology lab of the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research.

q: What breakthrough did Ebright achieve in his senior year by growing cells from a monarch's wing in a culture?
o: He turned viceroy wing scales into monarch scales
He proved wing cells grow fastest without sunlight
He showed wing cells divide and form normal butterfly wing scales only when fed the gold-spot hormone
He cloned a living monarch inside a test tube
e: In his senior year, Ebright grew cells from a monarch's wing in a culture and proved they divided into normal scales only if fed the hormone from the gold spots.

q: Where did Ebright go back after his freshman year at Harvard University to identify the hormone's chemical structure?
o: Pennsylvania State Medical Centre
University of Toronto zoology wing
Laboratory of the U.S. Department of Agriculture
Reading High School chemistry lab
e: After his freshman year at Harvard, Ebright returned to the Department of Agriculture laboratory and used sophisticated instruments to identify the hormone's chemical structure.

q: What exactly was Ebright looking at when he got the idea for his new theory about cell life?
o: Microscope slides of frog blood
X-ray photos of the chemical structure of a hormone
Migratory maps sent by Dr. Urquhart
Plastic wing models from his basement
e: A year and a half later, during his junior year, Ebright got the idea while looking at X-ray photos of the chemical structure of a hormone.

q: In what position did Richard Ebright graduate from Harvard University?
o: Second in his class of 1,510 with highest honours
First in his class of 800
Fifth in his class of 2,000
Tenth in a class of 500
e: Richard Ebright graduated from Harvard with highest honours, second in his class of 1,510, and became a graduate student researcher at Harvard Medical School.

q: What extracurricular activities did Richard Ebright excel in apart from science?
o: Chess, swimming, and oil painting
Stage acting, wrestling, and carpentry
Football, baseball, and violin
Debating, public speaking, canoeing, and photography
e: Ebright was also a champion debater and public speaker, a good canoeist and all-around outdoors-person, and an expert photographer.

q: Why were the two boys in London fascinated yet bewildered by the muddy footprints on the steps?
o: The footprints were twice the size of a normal elephant
The footprints moved upward along the vertical brick wall
A glowing green trail surrounded each muddy step
Fresh footprints appeared one after another with nobody visible making them
e: They saw fresh muddy imprints descending the steps and moving down the street, yet no person was visible anywhere.

q: Why was Griffin's invisibility both an advantage and a severe curse during his escape in London?
o: The drug permanently destroyed his eyesight in bright daylight
It prevented him from speaking aloud while invisible
He could evade capture only when naked, which left him freezing in mid-January cold
His invisible feet caused him to sink deep into asphalt roads
e: Clothes kept him warm but made him visible; stripping kept him invisible but exposed him to bitter mid-January winter cold.

q: What character flaw in Griffin is most clearly revealed when he attacks the Drury Lane shopkeeper from behind?
o: His extreme cowardice when confronting policemen
His callous ruthlessness and complete disregard for innocent people
His accidental clumsiness caused by poor vision
His selfless desire to fund scientific education
e: Attacking an innocent shopkeeper from behind and robbing his cash proves Griffin had no moral scruples and used science for selfish crime.

q: How did the stolen money from Drury Lane affect Mrs. Hall's initial attitude toward Griffin in Iping?
o: Advance payment persuaded her to tolerate his rudeness and eccentric secrecy
She demanded he share his chemical formula instead of rent
She suspected he had robbed the London store before arrival
She immediately reported him to the magistrate for carrying too much silver
e: Mrs. Hall overlooked his irritability and desire for solitude largely because he was an "eccentric scientist" who paid her in advance.

q: Why was the clergyman unable to catch the thief inside his study even though he heard the chink of money?
o: The room looked completely empty because Griffin was invisible
His wife dropped the poker and warned the burglar
The burglar locked the clergyman inside the bedroom
The thief escaped down the chimney before he entered
e: Even after searching under the desk, behind curtains, and up the chimney, the clergyman saw nobody because Griffin was standing invisibly inside.

q: Why did Mrs. Hall find the open bedroom door in the inn especially suspicious that morning?
o: The door had been broken down with an iron axe
Heavy snow had piled inside the hallway outside
The constable had warned her never to open guest doors
Griffin always kept the door shut and locked and grew furious if anyone entered
e: Griffin normally kept his door tightly shut and locked; seeing it wide open made Mr. and Mrs. Hall seize the rare opportunity to investigate.

q: What actually caused the hat to dash into Mrs. Hall's face and the chair to push the Halls out of the room?
o: Hidden springs built beneath the floorboards
A strong winter gust blowing through an open window
The invisible Griffin physically lifting and throwing them
Vengeful spirits haunting the old inn
e: Mrs. Hall mistook the flying objects for witchcraft, whereas it was actually the unseen Griffin defending his privacy and hiding place.

q: Why did Mrs. Hall emotionally mention "My poor mother used to sit in that chair!" after escaping the room?
o: She feared the chair would break and lose family value
She was horrified and heartbroken believing the stranger had bewitched her late mother's chair to attack her
She wanted Griffin to pay extra rent for using antique furniture
She remembered hiding savings inside the chair cushion
e: Her outburst reflects superstitious terror: she believed Griffin's witchcraft turned even a cherished family heirloom against her.

q: Why did the village constable Mr. Jaffers decide to proceed with the arrest even when Griffin had no head?
o: He thought Griffin was wearing an optical illusion mirror
His sense of duty told him a magistrate's warrant must be obeyed whether the suspect had a head or not
Mrs. Hall promised him half of the clergyman's stolen money
He did not notice Griffin's missing head in the dim bar light
e: Jaffers exemplified strict devotion to duty: if a magistrate's warrant ordered a person's arrest, that person had to be arrested with or without a head.

q: Why could the villagers helping Constable Jaffers not capture Griffin at the end of the story?
o: Griffin threw off his remaining garments and struck unseen blows from nowhere
Griffin bribed the villagers with notes from the clergyman's desk
The inn roof collapsed and blocked the exit
Griffin escaped by boarding a midnight train at Iping station
e: By shedding his shirt and trousers, Griffin became completely invisible, knocked Jaffers unconscious, and escaped amid confused cries of "Hold him!".

q: Which contrast best captures the irony in the title "Footprints Without Feet"?
o: Griffin wears thick boots everywhere so he never leaves bare footprints
The boys leave footprints while chasing an imaginary ghost
Shoes walk on their own across the London store
Muddy footprints are clearly visible on London steps, yet the feet and body making them cannot be seen
e: Normally footprints imply visible feet, but Griffin's invisibility leaves tangible muddy tracks with no visible feet attached.

q: If Griffin had used his discovery ethically like a true scientist, what could he have done instead of robbing and assaulting people?
o: Hidden permanently in theatrical shops across London
Used witchcraft rumours to frighten innocent innkeepers
Published his research transparently for medical, optical, or scientific advancement
Burned his landlord's house in secret every winter
e: A true scientist shares discoveries responsibly to benefit humanity, whereas Griffin turned an extraordinary breakthrough into a tool for vengeance and theft.

q: Why was Griffin forced to reveal himself as a headless figure to the people in the Iping inn bar?
o: His bandages accidentally caught fire near the stove
He wanted to apply for a stage role in Iping village
Mrs. Hall aggressively confronted him about the bewitched chair and locked room, making him lose his temper
The clergyman recognized his voice from the study robbery
e: Furious at Mrs. Hall's interrogation ("I want to know how it is you came out of an empty room"), Griffin snapped and tore off his disguise.

q: How does the London store episode highlight Griffin's greed beyond mere survival?
o: He swept the restaurant floor to repay the store owners
After warming and clothing himself, he indulged in cold meat, coffee, sweets, and wine before sleeping on quilts
He stayed only five minutes to borrow a single woollen scarf
He left a handwritten IOU note on the manager's counter
e: Instead of slipping out quietly once warm, Griffin feasted recklessly on stolen food and wine and overslept, revealing self-indulgence.

q: What does the phrase "extraordinary affair!" repeated by the clergyman all day suggest about the villagers' mindset?
o: They were totally baffled because visible theft occurred inside an apparently empty room
They were amused by an everyday prank played by village children
They suspected Mrs. Hall had stolen the clergyman's housekeeping cash
They immediately guessed a scientific invisibility drug existed
e: Since invisibility was beyond their imagination, seeing money vanish from an empty study seemed utterly inexplicable until witchcraft rumours arose.

q: How did Richard Ebright's mother ensure that his curiosity never faded after his father's death?
o: She forced him to memorize medical textbooks for ten hours daily
She forbade butterfly collecting so he would focus only on mathematics
She sent him away to a strict military boarding school
She bought microscopes, telescopes, cameras, took him on trips, and gave him learning tasks every evening
e: His mother nurtured his mind with equipment, trips, evening learning activities at the dining table, and "The Travels of Monarch X".

q: How did "The Travels of Monarch X" serve as a turning point in Ebright's childhood?
o: It taught him how to win prize money by selling rare butterflies
It warned him that monarchs were endangered and could not be studied
It inspired him to abandon biology and study Central American geography
It connected his hobby of collecting butterflies to real scientific migration research under Dr. Urquhart
e: By second grade he had collected all 25 local species and might have stopped, but the book invited readers to tag monarchs for Dr. Urquhart.

q: Why did Ebright win an award in eighth grade even though his caterpillar-beetle experiment yielded "no real results"?
o: He included colourful photographs of viceroy butterflies
The judges felt sorry for his defeat in seventh grade
He actually conducted and demonstrated a genuine scientific experiment rather than a mere display
His mother secretly persuaded the science fair committee
e: Showing that he had tested a hypothesis (whether a beetle carries the viral disease) through a real experiment demonstrated true scientific method.

q: In Ebright's viceroy-monarch experiment, what assumption did his starling test initially challenge?
o: That starlings eat only dry seeds and berries
That birds never eat monarch butterflies because monarchs taste bad to them
That monarchs migrate south only during winter storms
That viceroys are twice as large as monarchs
e: The theory assumed birds avoid monarchs for their bad taste, yet Ebright's starling ate all the monarchs it could get instead of ordinary bird food.

q: How did an investigation into "ornamental" gold spots on a monarch pupa unexpectedly lead to a breakthrough in human cell biology?
o: Those spots produced a hormone whose X-ray chemical structure later helped Ebright understand how cells read DNA
The gold spots contained microscopic human blood cells
Ebright sold the gold dust from pupae to fund Harvard Medical School
The pupae cured viral diseases in laboratory frogs
e: Discovering the gold-spot hormone led him to determine its chemical structure at the USDA lab, and X-ray photos of that hormone sparked his DNA cell theory.

q: What did Ebright's senior-year experiment of growing monarch wing cells in a culture prove beyond doubt?
o: The gold-spot hormone is essential for cells to divide and develop into normal wing scales
Butterfly wings can survive indefinitely without oxygen
Viceroy wing cells transform into monarch cells in sugar solution
Gold spots fade away if pupae are exposed to sunlight
e: Wing cells in culture divided and grew into normal butterfly wing scales ONLY when fed the hormone produced by the twelve gold spots.

q: Why did Ebright NOT shout "Eureka!" when he discovered the answer to how cells read DNA?
o: His roommate James Wong had already published the same idea
He was forbidden from making noise inside the library
He wasn't sure whether his discovery was important yet
Calm scientific insight built gradually from years of hormone research rather than sudden theatrics
e: The text notes he didn't shout "Eureka!"; instead, quiet conviction grew from combining his insect hormone findings with X-ray photos of chemical structure.

q: What comparison does the author use to highlight the rarity of Ebright and Wong publishing in the "Proceedings of the National Academy of Science"?
o: Winning a national chess championship blindfolded
Winning an Olympic gold medal in canoeing at age ten
Making the big leagues at age fifteen and hitting a home run the very first time at bat
Scoring a hat-trick in a World Cup football final
e: Since the journal had never before published college students' work, Peterson compares it to hitting a home run at your very first bat in the big leagues at fifteen.

q: How did Mr. Richard A. Weiherer distinguish between unhealthy rivalry and Ebright's "competitive spirit"?
o: Ebright never entered contests where prizes were offered
Ebright wasn't trying to win merely for a prize; he wanted to do the best job possible for the right reasons
Ebright let his debate opponents win whenever they looked tired
Ebright competed only in outdoor canoeing and never in academics
e: Weiherer explained Ebright was competitive not in a bad sense — he strove to be the best because he cared deeply about doing his best work.

q: Why did Ebright admire Mr. Weiherer as "the perfect person for me then"?
o: Mr. Weiherer wrote all his debate speeches for him
Mr. Weiherer opened his mind to new ideas and encouraged his extra effort in Debating and Model UN
Mr. Weiherer excused him from attending social studies classes

o: Because London shops charged double prices for coats in January
To show that Griffin was allergic to falling snow in Sussex
Because the boys only walked outside on chilly mornings
To mock Griffin's lack of foresight: despite his scientific brilliance, impulsive anger led him into a desperate, miserable trap
e: Acting out of vindictive rage against his landlord without planning for winter survival reveals how his hot temper undermined his intellect.

q: Consider the scene where Griffin pretends to wait for a cheque while actually planning the clergyman's robbery. What trait does this reinforce?
o: His remorse over stealing coins in Drury Lane
His reluctant honesty toward poor innkeepers
His calculating deceit and willingness to exploit others' trust to sustain his criminal lifestyle
His genuine expectation of a university research grant
e: Lying smoothly about an expected cheque while exploiting invisibility to rob a trusting clergyman's house confirms Griffin's manipulative nature.

q: How does the ending of "Footprints Without Feet" ("Griffin had shaken himself free, and no one knew where to lay hands on him") maintain suspense?
o: By revealing that Constable Jaffers secretly helped him escape
By confirming that Griffin quietly surrendered to London police the next morning
By leaving an intelligent, angry, and completely invisible fugitive still at large in the world
By showing Mrs. Hall discovering the secret formula under the bed
e: Unlike a tidy fairy-tale arrest, this open ending leaves the dangerous, invisible Griffin loose and unchecked, preserving the thriller tension of Wells's novel.

q: Evaluate the role of failure in "The Making of a Scientist". How did losing in seventh grade paradoxically produce Ebright's later Nobel-level calibre?
o: It forced him to abandon butterflies and copy another winner's astronomy project
It jolted him out of passive collecting/displaying and revealed that real science demands hypothesis-driven experiments
It made his mother hire private tutors to guarantee prizes every year
It discouraged him from ever using frog slides or microscopes again
e: Feeling sad while others won taught him the decisive distinction between neat displays and real experiments, catalyzing his partnership with Dr. Urquhart.

q: Look closely at Ebright's viceroy-monarch project: his starling ate monarchs, yet later researchers found viceroys probably DO mimic monarchs. What essential scientific truth does this illustrate?
o: Early experiments can produce unexpected or partial evidence that later, broader research refines without invalidating the experimenter's method
Starling birds are poor subjects for all biological studies
Viceroy butterflies changed their flavour over the next decade
Science fairs reward projects even when the student fabricates results
e: Science is self-correcting and cumulative: Ebright rigorously tested a hypothesis with a bird species (earning 1st in zoology), while later wider studies refined the ecological conclusion.

q: Why did Ebright's research chain — from butterfly tagging to pupa gold spots to cell culture to USDA hormone structure to DNA reading — succeed where isolated curiosity often fails?
o: Because he switched topics completely every six months without finishing old ones
Because Harvard University automatically publishes all freshman biology papers
Because he inherited a private chemical factory in Reading
Because each answered question naturally generated a deeper, connected question pursued with sustained discipline and institutional mentors
e: Every stage built cumulatively upon the previous discovery—ornamental spots led to a hormone, which led to wing scale growth, chemical structure, and finally DNA reading.

q: Examine the concluding recipe of the chapter: "Start with a first-rate mind, add curiosity, and mix in the will to win for the right reasons." Which option best explains why the third ingredient is indispensable?
o: Curiosity alone makes students fail their school social studies exams
The will to win means defeating lab partners before sharing credit
Only students who win international cash prizes are allowed into medical school
Without integrity and the drive to pursue excellence for truth rather than ego or prizes, intelligence and curiosity can easily go astray—as seen in characters like Griffin
e: Intellect plus curiosity without "winning for the right reasons" can degenerate into selfishness (like Griffin) or superficial prize-hunting; wanting to do one's best sustains ethical science.

q: In "The Making of a Scientist", why is it significant that Richard Ebright's mother was not a scientist herself, yet successfully nurtured one?
o: She prevented Richard from joining outdoor sports until college
She relied entirely on school detention punishments to enforce reading
She demonstrated that attentive encouragement, providing tools/books, and creating daily curiosity-rich challenges matter more than specialized degrees in early parenting
She hired Dr. Urquhart to live in Reading as Richard's private tutor
e: Through companionship after his father's death, buying equipment she could provide, and giving "The Travels of Monarch X", she fanned his innate curiosity into lifelong passion.

q: How does Ebright's collaboration with "another excellent science student" in tenth grade and with "James R. Wong" at Harvard refute a common stereotype about scientists?
o: That scientists only work in dusty dark basements without electric lighting
That major breakthroughs are made only by isolated lone geniuses rather than through open teamwork and shared dialogue
That college roommates never discuss academic biology outside lectures
That only senior professors above age fifty can co-author journal papers
e: From building the gold-spot device with a peer to working all night with James R. Wong on molecular models, Ebright thrived through collaboration—unlike secretive Griffin.

q: Ebright was a straight-A student, yet he still spent three or four extra hours at night doing debate research alongside butterfly experiments. What quality did Mr. Weiherer see in that habit?
o: Extraordinary dedication and intellectual hunger to prepare thoroughly in everything he undertook
Desire to escape cleaning butterfly cages in the basement
Disorganized time management that threatened his biology grades
Fear of failing Mr. Weiherer's social studies final examination
e: Weiherer praised him precisely because, despite already excelling in science and straight-A academics, Ebright poured wholehearted effort into debate research too.

q: Why was Dr. Frederick A. Urquhart's reply—"a stack of suggestions for experiments"—more valuable to an eighth grader than simply giving Ebright one finished answer?
o: Because it empowered Ebright with open questions that fuelled years of independent experiments across high school and international fairs
Because postage from Canada cost less for stacks of old lab paper
Because Ebright needed dozens of ideas just in case he failed seventh grade again
Because Dr. Urquhart did not know how monarch caterpillars developed
e: True mentorship gives young minds fertile questions rather than spoon-fed conclusions; Urquhart's stack of suggestions kept Ebright busy all through high school.

q: What makes Ebright's reaction upon seeing the hormone X-ray photos ("he didn't shout 'Eureka!'") so realistic and instructive about scientific discovery?
o: Scientists at Harvard were strictly trained never to speak aloud inside labs
Ebright disliked ancient Greek words like "Eureka" used by Archimedes
He immediately doubted whether X-ray machines could photograph liquid hormones
Great breakthroughs rarely come from blind luck; they emerge when a prepared mind recognizes how new evidence fits years of prior puzzle pieces
e: It wasn't a theatrical sudden miracle; years of butterfly hormone experiments prepared Ebright's mind to recognize DNA reading instantly in those X-ray photos.

q: Why does the author call DNA "the blueprint for life" when explaining Ebright and Wong's theory?
o: Because only blue monarch wings contain genetic material inside their scales
Because DNA appears bright blue under an ordinary high-school microscope
Because just as an architect's blueprint carries complete instructions for building a structure, DNA in the nucleus controls heredity and determines every cell's form and function
Because Watson and Crick drew the first DNA diagram on blue drafting paper
e: The metaphor of a "blueprint" captures how DNA encodes hereditary instructions in the nucleus, and Ebright's theory explained how the cell "reads" that blueprint.

q: How did Ebright convert a setback in his monarch tagging work (only 2 butterflies recaptured within 75 miles) into forward momentum rather than quitting science?
o: He forged higher recapture numbers on his county science fair charts
He wrote to Dr. Urquhart for experimental questions and shifted from tedious tagging to laboratory biology projects at science fairs
He moved permanently to Central America to catch the remaining monarchs himself
He stopped studying insects altogether and took up full-time canoe racing
e: When tagging proved tedious with little feedback and seventh-grade display failed, he pivoted toward hypothesis-driven experiments guided by Urquhart's suggestions.

q: Look at the progression of venues in Ebright's research: basement -> county science fair -> International Science Fair -> Walter Reed Army lab -> USDA lab -> Harvard. What does this trajectory demonstrate?
o: Big breakthroughs begin only inside billion-dollar university laboratories
Humble home-grown curiosity, when paired with rigour and opportunity, can scale step by step to world-class institutional science
High school fairs were far harder to win than Harvard honours
Army laboratories exclusively recruit butterfly collectors from Pennsylvania
e: Ebright started with cardboard tags and eggs in his basement, yet disciplined progression opened doors to elite federal research labs and Harvard Medical School.

q: Which pair of traits best captures the fundamental contrast between Griffin ("Footprints Without Feet") and Richard Ebright ("The Making of a Scientist")?
o: Vindictive secrecy and lawless abuse of knowledge vs collaborative curiosity and ethical pursuit of excellence
Experimental failure vs accidental luck without hard work
Physical invisibility vs public political leadership
Wealthy nobleman vs impoverished village boy
e: Placing both chapters side by side reveals the twin faces of scientific talent: Griffin destroys trust through secrecy and crime; Ebright elevates society through openness and integrity.

q: Why does Peterson mention that Ebright was "an expert photographer, particularly of nature and scientific exhibits"?
o: Because photography was a compulsory event at the International Science Fair
To explain how he sold wildlife photos to pay for his Harvard tuition
Because he photographed Griffin's footprints during a trip to London
To show that keen observation, precision, and visual documentation strengthened both his artistic hobbies and his scientific exhibits
e: Keen visual observation in nature photography complemented his skill in preparing scientific exhibits and later interpreting molecular X-ray photos.

q: What irony exists in the fact that Griffin, who made himself invisible so nobody could catch or control him, ended up constantly trapped by basic human needs?
o: He had to hire Constable Jaffers to bring him meals from the kitchen
He spent all his money buying butterfly cages in Drury Lane
He became dependent on stealing food, coats, bandages, and cash from visible society just to survive each winter day
He was legally required to pay double rent to Mrs. Hall for two rooms
e: Far from achieving godlike independence, Griffin remained bound by hunger, cold, and the need for money—forcing him into petty thefts inside a visible world.
